G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
The major mechanism of corrosion inhibition effect by nicotinic acid (NA) is to form a passivation film which adsorbs on cobalt (Co) surface so as to strengthen the
surface impedance and isolate the corrosion medium. In an alkaline environment (pH 10), NA exists in the form of Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions, which are negatively charged. Driven
by electrostatic forces and Van der Waals forces between NA molecule (N atom and the carboxyl) and cobalt atom, Nic<sup>2−</sup> ions are appealed to the Co(OH)<sub>2</sub>, leading to
the appearance of Co(II)-NA molecule groups. NA molecules produce a single or multilayer self-assembled Co(II)-NA film on the cobalt surface and further preven
the corrosion on Co film.

1. Introduction
As the feature size of integrated circuits (ICs) shrinks below 10 nm,
cobalt is the most promising material to replace tungsten (W) and copper
(Cu) as the front and intermediate lines owing to its great resistance to
electromigration and good performance in step coverage [1]. In addi-
tion, the barrier layer of cobalt interconnect ICs is thinner than that of
copper [2,3]. After cobalt film deposition, the wafer surface is uneven,
so chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is used in IC manufacturing
process to realize local and global planarization through the coordina
tion of chemical action and mechanical action [4].
However, Co is prone to being corroded by CMP slurry, which con
tains many aggressive chemicals, e.g., oxidizers and complexing agents,
in which
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }
is widely used to increase removal rate of cobalt as a
green oxidizer [5,6]. Yang et al. [7] studied the corrosion of Co in
alkaline medium containing
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }
and found that lots of pits were
appeared in the presence of 0.1 wt%
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,
, and at some locations, the
coating layer was fragmented and peeling occurred. In order to reduce
the corrosion of Co surface, many methods and new chemicals have been
introduced into the study of cobalt. Badawy et al. [8] investigated the
corrosion of Co in alkaline solution and suggested that the potential of
Co can be increased by increasing the pH value of the solution to slow
down the corrosion rate. Accordingly, all experiments in this study were
carried out under alkaline conditions.
In recent years, the addition of corrosion inhibitors has been proved
to be an effective measure to inhibit corrosion of metal materials [9 11].
Many studies show that organic inhibitor molecules containing elements
such as C, N, and O are often more effective in corrosion prevention,
among which benzotriazole (BTA) is a common inhibitor and has been
broadly commercialized [12 14]. The corrosion inhibition effect of BTA
was firstly reported by Cotton et al. [15], and since then researchers
have carried out a lot of researches on BTA
. However, some
current studies reported that BTA has a poor inhibition effect on Co
corrosion in corrosive medium. Yang et al. [7] characterized the surface
morphology of Co in the solution containing BTA and
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }
by SEM, and
concluded that BTA could not effectively reduce the pitting caused by
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }
on Co surface. Similarly, Lei et al. [18] suggested that BTA is no
longer applicable to Co CMP by means of surface morphology test. In
addition, the toxicity of BTA also limits its application in CMP [19,20].
Therefore, scholars have been committed to developing green and
effective corrosion inhibitors for Co CMP, such as organic acid and vi
tamins [21–23].
Notably, nicotinic acid, which belongs to the B3 group of vitamins, is
widely used as an intermediate in the synthesis of various pharmaceu-
ticals and shows favorable potential in corrosion inhibition effect.
Mohamed et al. [23] investigated the polishing behavior and defects of
cobalt samples with an aqueous mixture of
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,
oxalic acid (OA), and
nicotinic acid at pH 10. The results show that the alkaline solution
including 80 mM NA can broadly reduce the corrosion current of cobalt
samples and galvanic erosion between cobalt and copper, proving that
NA can operate as an inhibitor for Co film in
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }
solution. He et al. [24]
concluded that NA offers a composite layer on the cobalt surface, and
prevents further Co corrosion, while a combination of 10 mM NA and 5
mM TAZ minimized Co-Cu corrosion as measured by zero resistance
galvanometer. Although it is confirmed that NA possesses an inhibition
effect on cobalt, further studies on NA, such as the interaction process
between NA and
\mathrm { C o } ,
the adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface and
so on, have not been reported. Studying the adsorption of corrosion
inhibitor on the metal surface is of great significance to explore the
corrosion inhibition mechanism. This work mainly studies the inhibitory
effect of NA on cobalt corrosion in alkaline medium, as well as the
formation and mechanism of [NA-Co] complex.
Studies on the performance of inhibitor molecules only by conven-
tional chemical experiments and characteristic methods are inadequate.
The rapid development of theoretical chemistry provides a more scien-
tific explanation for its research. Molecular simulation is a crucial
approach to study the molecular chemical activity of corrosion in-
hibitors from a microscopic perspective [25,27–29]. The adsorption
mechanism between inhibitors and metal substrates can be intuitively
characterized by molecular simulation technology. Ma et al. [26] probed
the effect of potassium oleate (PO) as a viable corrosion inhibitor for Cu
films in
\mathrm { E D T A  – H _ { 2 } O _ { 2 } }
based solution through combining chemical
experiment analysis with molecular simulation. Density functional
theory and molecular dynamics approaches were applied to study the
inhibition mechanism at the atom level of PO on Cu(111) substrate. Yin
et al. [16] evaluated the corrosion inhibition of BTA and TAZ at the
molecular level via comparing quantum chemical descriptors. There-
fore, it is necessary to further study the quantum chemical properties of
NA and micro adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface.
Considering that NA is an inexpensive, green, and easily available
organic inhibitor, it was introduced into the alkaline (pH 10) solution.
The molecular structure of NA is shown in Fig. 1. Contact angle and PDP
measurements were carried out to determine the optimal concentration
of NA. The passive film of NA was investigated by EIS, and the reaction
between Co and NA was explored by XPS. Density functional theory was
employed to study the properties of NA molecule. Several chemical
descriptors were calculated to reveal active sites of NA molecule and the
electron transfer characteristics between NA and Co atoms, as well as
MD simulation was conducted to study the adsorption configuration,
adsorption stability and adsorption sites of NA on Co surface. This work
provides a more in-depth insight into the development of alkaline cobalt
CMP slurry.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Contact angle test analysis
The adsorption of organic molecules on the metal surface will change
its hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity and alters the contact angle of metal
surface, while fresh metal surfaces usually present hydrophilicity, hence
the contact angle reflects the adsorption effect of the inhibitor [30].
Fig. 2 illustrates contact angle of cobalt samples treated with different
concentrations of NA and compared with that treated with CA. After CA
treatment, the natural oxide layer on the cobalt surface was removed,
and the contact angle of the cobalt surface reduced from
5 5 ^ { \circ }
obtaining the fresh cobalt surface [31]. The contact angle increased to
6 7 ^ { \circ }
following 40 mM NA treatment and increased steadily with the in-
crease of NA concentration until the maximum contact angle reached
8 3 ^ { \circ }
when the concentration was 80 mM. When the concentrations of NA
were 90 and 100 mM, the contact angles were 82◦ and 83◦, respectively,
which remained basically unchanged compared with that of 80 mM.
These results show that when the concentration of NA is greater than
80 mM, the adsorption of NA molecules on the cobalt surface reaches
saturation.
3.2. Electrochemical test analysis
According to the contact angle results, PDP tests were carried out to
evaluate the effect of corrosion inhibition of NA with the concentration
less than 100 mM on cobalt electrode. Fig. 3 shows the PDP curves of
cobalt electrode treated with different NA concentrations.
With the introduction of NA, both the anode and cathode branches of
Tafel curves have the tendency to extend to the region of low corrosion
current density. Compared with the cathode branches, the corrosion
current density of the anode branches differs from one another mark-
edly, i.e. the reduction reaction rate of dissolved oxygen at the cathode
basically remains unchanged, while the metal ionization process
occurring at the anode is inhibited. Accordingly, nicotinic acid belongs
to the anodic corrosion inhibitor. The linear region of anodic branch,
named as passivation region, proves that NA molecules gradually adhere
to the cobalt surface to form a protective film and reduce the corrosion
degree. It is noteworthy that the slope at the end of the 40 mM NA anode
branch (circled in red) sinks, which is caused by the incompactness of
the passivation film as the local corrosion medium may interact with the
metal through the protective layer to aggravate the metal ionization.
The illustration in Fig. 3 shows the PDP test curves of cobalt electrode in
NA solutions with concentrations of 80, 90 and 100 mM, respectively. It
can be seen that these three curves almost coincide, which indicates the
surface corrosion of Co electrode is similar.

3.3. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy analysis
EIS measurement was used to analyze the passivation effect of
physically adsorbed protective film on cobalt surface in alkaline me-
dium. Fig. 5(a) shows the Nyquist impedance spectra of the Co elec-
trodes in different concentrations of NA, which can better understand
the structure of passivation layer. Since the Nyquist curve is a 1/4 arc,
the charge transfer controls the erosion on cobalt/alkaline medium
interface, and the equivalent circuit is a simple model formed by elec-
tron exchange on passivation film. In the event that the general shape of
the impedance spectra does not change with the introduction of in-
hibitors, the reaction principle of the corrosive medium could be
considered as unaffected [35]. Meanwhile the radius of the spectrum
increases with the increase of NA concentration, suggesting that the
adsorption film turns to be more completed [36]. The radius of imped
ance spectrum reaches the maximum when the concentration of NA is
80 mM, which is consistent with PDP results. Nonetheless, the center of
the 1/4 arc is apparently below the x-axis, known as the frequency
dispersion effect, which is on account of the non-ideal capacitive
behavior of the cobalt/medium interface generated by the
non-uniformity of cobalt electrode surface.
It is necessary to immerse the cobalt sample for adequate time to
ensure the penetration of electrolyte into the film approach saturation.
Then the Q value of the phasing element in the circuit will basically
remain stable when the measured resistance can more precisely reflect
the impedance change of the film [8].

4. Conclusion
In this work, we focused on nicotinic acid as a potential corrosion
inhibitor for cobalt CMP in alkaline medium, and the adsorption
behavior of NA was systematically revealed by several characteristic
techniques and molecular simulations. The results of contact angel and
electrochemical test show that corrosion efficiency reached the
maximum value of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM. The
adsorption of NA on cobalt surface follows the Langmuir adsorption
isotherm, which is a spontaneous physical process. EIS further suggests
that with the increase of NA concentration, the passivation film covered
on cobalt surface became more complete, resulting in the increase of
surface resistance. According to the results of XPS, NA molecules exist in
the form of
\mathrm { N i c } ^ { 2 - }
ions in alkaline environment, and physically assemble
on
\mathrm { C o ( O H ) _ { 2 } }
to form Co(II)-NA molecular groups to isolate the perme-
ation of corrosive medium. DFT calculation and MD simulation indicate
that NA molecule is adsorbed on the Co(111) surface at a certain angle
through Coulomb force and van der Waals force, which are derived from
the interaction of
\mathrm { N } { = } \mathrm { C }
bond and carboxyl in NA molecule and surface
cobalt atoms. The results of this work on passive film of NA on Co surface
and its microscopic properties provide a theoretical basis for optimizing
the composition of Co CMP slurry, and also provide support for subse-
quent researches of exploring synergistic effect of NA and other slurry
components. In conclusion, NA is suggested to be an effective potential
inhibitor for Co CMP in IC manufacturing process. Its physical adsorp-
tion on cobalt surface will help to improve the inhibitor removal effect in
post CMP cleaning.
